                           WHEN I WAS ASKED TO RECUSE...

                          1.     While I began to pen this judgment in the quiet aftermath of
                          end of arguments, the Courtroom had fallen silent, the voices of
                          arguments had faded, the echoes of accusations no longer filled the
                          courtroom or my ears, what remained was the quiet weight of
                          responsibility of being a Judge, who has taken oath on the
                          Constitution of India i.e. Bharat, to uphold the purity and dignity of
                          the judicial system, with one persistent question - „Should I recuse?‟

                          2.     It was also that moment, when I realized that my silence as a
                          judge itself is being put to test - and now the question is no longer
                          about the case, but about the judge and fairness of the process and
                          institution itself.

                          3.     While in my entire life, as in the lives of many of my brother
                          and sister judges across this country, the cases put up before us for
                          adjudication test our knowledge, intellect and experience, at times
                          before few of us, a litigant through a case, tests the institution‟s
                          resilience itself. This case belongs to the latter category.

                          4.     The challenge before me was not that I had to adjudicate
                          difficult questions of law or fact, but I was drawn to adjudicate a
                          recusal application against myself. However, it is not for the first
                          time that such an application has been filed before the same judge
                          seeking recusal by a litigant. Therefore, in that sense, it is not an
                          extraordinary situation for a judge. In the past, before this High Court
                          itself, there have been multiple occasions when applications for

By:ZEENAT PRAVEEN

                           recusal have been filed before the same judge, which have been
                          heard and decided by them.

                          5.     The issue before me was clear - as to whether I should recuse
                          from hearing the present case. I was thus faced with a situation where
                          my impartiality and dignity had been challenged, and the natural
                          instinct would have been to recuse without hearing the application
                          seeking recusal, which would have been the easier path of
                          withdrawing and stepping aside. However, for the sake of the
                          institution, I decided to adjudicate the recusal application, for it
                          throws questions not only at me, but also at the institution itself. It
                          also weighed in my mind that all my brother and sister Judges and
                          the judges of District Courts of Delhi, who are part of this institution,
                          may be affected by the outcome of this application since it may be
                          cited as a precedent and many other litigants may take a similar path.

                          6.     Equally was it clear to me that I had to decide it totally
                          undisturbed and unaffected by the accusations and insinuations, in a
                          fair manner, as objectively as it is required of a judge, and to test the
                          recusal applications purely on the basis of jurisprudence of recusal
                          laid down till date in our country, for that is what I have been trained
                          to do as a Judge and what I have lived in the last 34 years of my
                          judicial career.

                          7.     During arguments, the applicants repeatedly submitted before
                          the Court that they do not doubt my integrity on any account and

                           they are seeking recusal not because they doubt my integrity, but
                          because of apprehension in their own minds that I may be biased.

                          8.     What is also important is the fact that today I am dealing with
                          the apprehension in the mind of the litigant and not actual bias in
                          myself, which needed a thorough examination.

                          9.     What made the task more challenging was that, during
                          arguments, contrary stands were taken. All the applicants, at the
                          beginning of arguments on recusal and some in the pleadings as well,
                          submitted before this Court that they have complete respect for this
                          Court as an individual judge and they do not doubt integrity of any
                          kind or fairness of this Court. However, the applicants still want the
                          case to be transferred, not because I am biased, but because they
                          have apprehension in their mind that I may be biased.

                          10.    I am fully conscious of the fact that today, I am not to judge
                          the litigant, but the litigant has put me and this institution on trial,
                          and it will be dealt with as it should be, not only on my behalf but on
                          behalf of the institution of judiciary itself. To reiterate, though
                          choosing the path of recusal - without even hearing the application
                          for recusal - would have been quiet, comfortable, uncontroversial
                          and easy, but a reputation once surrendered to accusation of bias, if
                          not dealt with, will not be easy to re-claim.

                          11.    Therefore, I choose the path to resolve the controversy thrown
                          at me where my integrity has been put to test. The strength of judicial
                          institution lies in strong resolve to respond appropriately to such

                           accusations, fearlessly and unhesitatingly. It is with this resolve that I
                          begin writing my judgment and deal with every accusation hurled at
                          me in an objective manner, without being affected by any of it.

                          SUBMISSIONS BEFORE THE COURT

                          1.      In the present case, six of the respondents, i.e. discharged
                          accused persons, have sought the recusal of this Court from hearing
                          the present matter. These applicants are as under:

                          (i)     Respondent No. 3 [ACCUSED_2]
                          (ii)    Respondent No. 5 [ACCUSED_3]
                          (iii)   Respondent No. 8 [ACCUSED_4]
                          (iv)    Respondent No. 12 [ACCUSED_5]
                          (v)     Respondent No. 18 [ACCUSED_6]
                          (vi)    Respondent No. 19 [ACCUSED_7]

                          Submissions By Respondent No. 18 [ACCUSED_6]

                          2.      The applicant Sh. [ACCUSED_6], who appears in person,
                          states that he, in his mind, has an apprehension of bias, which
                          becomes the focal point in a case where a party seeks recusal of a
                          Judge. To buttress his submission, he relies upon the decision of the
                          Hon‟ble Supreme Court in [OTHER_2] v. Union of India: (1987)
                          4 SCC 611.

                          3.      He draws the attention of this Court to the order dated
                          09.03.2026 passed in the present case and states that on the very first
                          date the matter was listed, after hearing the Central Bureau of

                           Investigation [hereafter „CBI‟] only for „five minutes‟, this Court
                          observed that prima facie there appeared to be certain erroneous
                          observations in the discharge order passed by the learned Trial Court,
                          which had heard the accused persons for nearly three months and had
                          examined more than 40,000 pages of evidence. He states that since
                          the order dated 09.03.2026 was passed in the absence of any of the
                          accused persons or their counsels, it has given rise to an

                          present case are similar; rather, according to him, his apprehension is
                          on a stronger footing than the apprehension expressed by the
                          Directorate of Enforcement [hereafter „DoE‟] in that case.

                          5.     The Applicant Sh. [ACCUSED_6] also relies upon the
                          decision in [OTHER_3] v. State (NCT of Delhi): (2015) 6 SCC 617, to

                          attention of this Court to the decision [ACCUSED_6] v.

                          observations, such as those relating to non-recovery of the alleged

                          6.     Further, the Applicant Sh. [ACCUSED_6] submits that the
                          strong findings recorded by this Court in the past are totally contrary

                          order, which were arrived at after hearing the case for three months

                          findings recorded by the learned Trial Court are completely contrary

                          7.     He also draws the attention of this Court to the order passed by
                          this Court on the bail application filed by Respondent No. 8, i.e., the
                          decision in [ACCUSED_4] v. Enforcement Directorate: 2024 SCC
                          OnLine Del 3731, and submits that strong observations were made in
                          the said bail order and that this Court had almost held him guilty for

                          submits that since this Court has already made up its mind in respect
                          of the case in question, he apprehends that he will not get justice
                          from this Court.

                           8.     He also draws the attention of this Court, particularly to
                          paragraph no. 8 of the order dated 09.03.2026 passed in the present
                          case, and submits that this Court had observed as follows: "The
                          observations made by the learned Trial Court regarding the
                          statements of the witnesses and the approvers, at the stage of charge
                          itself, prima facie appear erroneous and require consideration when
                          viewed in the background of well-settled law on charge and
                          conspiracy, as to whether such observations could have been made at
                          the stage of charge itself." According to him, by recording these
                          observations, this Court has, at the very threshold, and without
                          hearing the accused persons and without going through the record,
                          given a finding that the order of the learned Trial Court is erroneous.
                          He further submits that the case of the prosecution is primarily based
                          on the statements of the approvers, and that this Court has already
                          recorded an observation in paragraph 8 of the order dated 09.03.2026
                          in this regard; therefore, he apprehends that he will not get justice
                          from this Court. He also submits that even the Trial Court Record
                          had not been summoned by this Court at that stage, and without
                          having the same before it, the Court had prima facie recorded
                          conclusions regarding the evidentiary value of the approvers‟
                          statements.

                          granted three to six months‟ time for filing replies, whereas in the

                          "Though this Court had granted opportunity to the respondents on
                          two occasions to file their replies to the main petition, some of the

                          15.    He also states that the impugned order was passed by the
                          learned Trial Court on 27.02.2026 and within four hours of the
                          passing of that order, the CBI chose to file a revision petition,
                          without specifically countering the observations made by the learned

                          a sweeping order on the basis of such a general petition filed before

                          16.    He further states that on the last date of hearing, this Court was
                          inclined to close the right of several accused persons to file their

                           mind that this Court may be more inclined or sympathetic towards
                          them, and therefore he doubts that he will not get justice from this
                          Court. When asked by this Court whether it had ever made any
                          political statement or any statement regarding the ideology followed
                          by the said Adhivakta Parishad, he stated that the mere fact that this
                          Court had attended a programme organised by the said Adhivakta
                          Parishad gives rise to a strong apprehension in his mind that he will
                          not get justice from this Court.

                          18.    He also states at the Bar, though it is not mentioned in the
                          pleadings, that the Union Minister of Home Affairs of this country
                          had made a statement in a television programme that when the
                          judgment of this Court comes, Sh. [ACCUSED_6] will have to approach the
                          Hon‟ble Supreme Court. According to him, this statement has given
                          rise to a suspicion in his mind that this Court will not give justice to

documents.title: Delhi Excise Policy: Court Discharges [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4] And Others In CBI Case
documents.text: A Delhi court on Friday discharged former Chief Minister [ACCUSED_6] and Aam Aadmi Party leader [ACCUSED_4], holding that the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) failed to make out a prima facie case against them. The order was passed by Special Judge Jitender Singh at the Rouse Avenue Courts, who refused to frame charges against any of the 23 accused persons in the matter and discharged them all. In a detailed order, the court criticised the investigation conducted by the CBI, observing that the agency had implicated the accused without sufficient material. The judge noted that the voluminous chargesheet contained several lacunae and was not supported by witness statements or substantive evidence. With respect to [ACCUSED_4], the court held that the CBI had failed to establish a prima facie case warranting the framing of charges. As regards [ACCUSED_6], the judge observed that he had been implicated without any cogent material on record. The case pertains to alleged irregularities in the formulation and implementation of the now-scrapped Delhi excise policy, which the CBI had claimed resulted in undue benefits to certain entities. The agency had filed a comprehensive chargesheet naming multiple accused, including political functionaries and other individuals. However, upon consideration of the material placed before it, the court concluded that the prosecution had not met the threshold required for proceeding to trial. Consequently, it declined to frame charges and discharged all 23 accused. All the 23 accused include: [ACCUSED_1], [ACCUSED_10], [ACCUSED_2], [ACCUSED_11], [ACCUSED_12], [ACCUSED_13], [ACCUSED_14], [ACCUSED_4], [ACCUSED_8], [ACCUSED_15], [ACCUSED_16], [ACCUSED_5], [ACCUSED_17], [ACCUSED_18], [ACCUSED_19], [ACCUSED_20], [ACCUSED_21] @ [ACCUSED_21], [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_7], [ACCUSED_22], [ACCUSED_23], [ACCUSED_24], and [ACCUSED_25]. Notably, in May 2025, the court had directed the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to provide a detailed list of all notices, summons, and written communications issued in the Delhi Excise Policy case, along with any responses received, to be included either in the list of relied-upon documents or unrelied documents (URDs). Special Judge (PC Act) Dig Vinay Singh had ruled on May 22 that if the CBI does not intend to rely on these documents during trial, they must be included in the URD list, which shall be made available for inspection by the accused. The Judge had also directed the Investigating Officer (IO) to file an affidavit confirming that no such document has been omitted. Additionally, the IO must clarify through a separate affidavit whether any search and seizure memos have been excluded from the URDs, as alleged by accused [ACCUSED_8]. "If any such search and seizure memos are missing from the URD list, they are to be added. Conversely, if none are omitted, the IO must file an affidavit to that effect," the court had said. The CBI had opposed the plea, arguing that such communications form part of the case diaries and not evidence per se, hence they are not subject to disclosure. The court had however, rejected this argument, holding that these documents do not fall under the protection of Section 172 of the CrPC. In a related news, in January the court had dismissed two complaints filed by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) against Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) leader and former Delhi Chief Minister [ACCUSED_6] for allegedly ignoring summons issued in connection with the Delhi excise policy investigation, holding that no incriminating material was made out against him. The ED had approached the Court in February 2024, seeking action against [ACCUSED_6] for not appearing before the agency despite five summons issued during the course of its money laundering probe linked to the now-scrapped Delhi Excise Policy for 2021–22. The agency alleged non-compliance with statutory summons requiring personal appearance and cooperation in the investigation. The ED's case stemmed from a money laundering probe initiated on August 22, 2022, following a First Information Report registered by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on August 17, 2022. The CBI case was based on a complaint by Delhi Lieutenant Governor V.K. Saxena alleging irregularities in the formulation and implementation of the excise policy. [ACCUSED_6] was subsequently arrested in the ED case earlier this year and later granted bail by the Supreme Court. Case Title: Central Bureau of Investigation v. [ACCUSED_1] & Ors. documents.title: "Tell Me What's Wrong With It": Delhi High Court To CBI on Discharge Of [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4] In Liquor Policy Case
documents.text:
Delhi High Court asked the CBI to identify precisely what was wrong with the trial court's order discharging [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4] and all other accused in the excise policy case, and listed the matter on November 5

While hearing the Central Bureau of Investigation's challenge to the discharge of former Delhi Chief Minister [ACCUSED_6], former Deputy Chief Minister [ACCUSED_4] and all other accused in the excise policy case, the Delhi High Court on Wednesday pressed the agency to point out specific errors in the trial court's order rather than restate its allegations.

"The judge has painstakingly gone through everything. Tell me what's wrong with it," Justice Sachin Datta told Additional Solicitor General (ASG) SV Raju.

At the close of the hearing, the Court directed the CBI to file fresh written submissions in a tabular format, setting out each paragraph of the impugned order under challenge, the findings disputed, and whether the complaint was that the wrong legal test had been applied or that material on record had been ignored or misread. The matter will next be heard on November 5 at 2:30 PM.

At the outset, the Court asked the ASG for an overview of the case. "Give me an overview of the case, what is the case against them," Justice Datta said.

When Raju sought to begin with the issue of maintainability, the Court declined. "No, on maintainability I'll hear them first. You give me a broad overview of the case," Justice Datta said.

Noting that the record was now before it and that preliminary objections had been raised, the Court emphasised that, in revisional jurisdiction, it had to examine whether there was anything palpably wrong with the order under challenge. It questioned the challenge to an order running into over 500 pages and asked counsel to identify the specific deficiencies that warranted interference, pointing to the relevant portions of the order and explaining how the challenge fell within the limited scope of revision.

Raju began by referring to the CBI's allegation that the policy was changed to facilitate the exchange of money before tenders and licences were awarded, allegedly enabling the accused and their associates to use the money for illegal purposes. The Court, however, asked him to move beyond the allegations and identify precisely what was wrong with the impugned order, given that the judge appeared to have examined the record in considerable detail.

Raju argued that the trial court, despite passing an order running into over 500 pages, had ignored crucial evidence and misinterpreted witness statements. Taking the Court to page 41 of his written submissions, he referred to allegations concerning suggestions attributed to the Lieutenant Governor, witness testimonies and file notings relating to the changes in the policy.

According to the CBI, the Lieutenant Governor had suggested only that the power to make changes in the policy should remain with the Council of Ministers, rather than being delegated to the Additional Advocate General. Raju argued that no other changes were suggested by the Lieutenant Governor, yet subsequent file notings recorded seven changes attributed to discussions with him, including a reduction in the turnover criteria.

He alleged that the policy was approved by the Council of Ministers through circulation on May 21, 2021, with unusual haste, while members of the alleged South Group were present in Delhi during the COVID wave. The reduction of the turnover criterion to ₹150 crore, he argued, benefited M/s Indospirit in obtaining an L-1 licence.

The ASG submitted that the trial court ignored a crucial statement of [WITNESS_1], [WITNESS_1], who allegedly stated that only the broad policy framework was discussed and no figures were discussed in the relevant section. This omission was significant, Raju argued, because the changes recorded in the file concerned figures such as the turnover criteria and shop size.

Raju then raised the alleged disappearance of an earlier draft Cabinet note dated January 28, 2021, which, according to the CBI, contained legal opinions recommending that the status quo in the excise policy be maintained. He alleged that when these opinions did not suit the accused's plan, a fresh file was initiated without incorporating them.

Referring to witness statements, emails, file notings and mobile phone chats, the ASG argued that the earlier draft Cabinet note and the accompanying legal opinions were handed over to the concerned authorities but subsequently disappeared from the record. A fresh Cabinet note was then prepared, he submitted, incorporating only a summary of comments and omitting any reference to the earlier file and the legal opinions.

Raju contended that the trial court selectively read the witness statements and misinterpreted the evidence on this aspect, and that the CBI's case was that the opinions favouring the status quo were excluded because they did not support the alleged plan to change the policy.

At this point, the Court sought to distil the ASG's grievance. "So, in a single sentence, your difficulty with this order is that this entire evidentiary exercise is done at the stage of charge?" Justice Datta asked.

Raju agreed, arguing that the trial court had gone beyond the permissible scope of scrutiny at that stage. The Court asked him to show the law on what a court is required to do at the stage of charge, observing that it could not simply substitute one opinion for another, and asked counsel to establish why the impugned order warranted interference in revisional jurisdiction.

Raju clarified that his argument was not that the trial court must act as a "rubber stamp", but that it could not ignore relevant evidence or misinterpret it. "If the court has considered it and then given a finding, which is a reasonable finding, then it's a different matter," he submitted. He maintained that the trial court had completely ignored relevant material and said the points raised were only the beginning of his challenge, adding that he would demonstrate further instances of evidence allegedly overlooked.

Taking the Court through the impugined order in FIR 405, Raju asked it to compare the undertaking extracted by the trial court with the original undertaking submitted by Indo Spirit Marketing Pvt Ltd. Pointing to the last two lines, he alleged that the order added the name of Indo Spirit Distribution Ltd, which did not appear in the original document.

"How could the learned judge tweak a document and extract something which was not there, part of the document?" Raju asked. He also argued that the alleged addition was significant because it was relied upon to conclude that the South Group did not benefit from the excise policy.

Raju further urged the Court to examine the relevant judgments rather than rely on selective readings of isolated paragraphs of the impugined order.

Citing the Supreme Court's judgment in [OTHER_17] v. CBI (as cited by counsel), he read out the principle that, at the stage of framing charges or considering discharge, the court is not expected to analyse the acceptability of evidence as it would at trial. The credibility of witnesses and the veracity of documents, he submitted, were matters to be assessed during trial, and the trial court had exceeded the permissible scope by undertaking an extensive evidentiary evaluation at the stage of charge.

Taking the Court through his chart, Raju alleged that the trial court overlooked evidence pointing to the role of the South Group in drafting the excise policy, including a 36-page printout, a meeting with accused [ACCUSED_2] and digital records tracing the movement of the persons involved.

According to the ASG, the evidence showed that 36 pages were printed at the Oberoi hotel, after which a taxi was hired to travel to Oberoi Meadows, where members of the South Group allegedly met [ACCUSED_2] and handed over the material. The final policy, he argued, subsequently contained the same 36 pages. He pointed to GPS records of the hired taxi and call detail records which, he said, placed the relevant person at the locations after the printout was taken.

Raju also relied on WhatsApp chats recovered from the phone of [OTHER_16], submitting that certain paragraphs in the chats predated the policy but were identical to provisions that later appeared in the final excise policy. Referring to one paragraph of the final policy, he argued that the corresponding provision appeared in the recovered chats despite allegedly not being part of the earlier draft, and that the trial court failed to properly account for this digital evidence.

The ASG alleged that the policy increased the profit margin for private wholesalers from 5% to 12%, despite the Dawan Committee recommending a 5% margin and wholesale operations through government-owned entities. The shift from government entities to private wholesalers, coupled with the increased margin, he argued, conferred an undue financial benefit on private operators and formed a crucial part of the prosecution's case. He took the Court to a paragraph of the first supplementary chargesheet which, he said, specifically recorded the change and the departure from the committee's recommendations.

The Court, however, asked counsel to identify the precise provision in the final excise policy that fixed the margin at 12%, seeking to examine the policy itself rather than rely solely on the allegations in the chargesheet. Raju maintained that the margin was arbitrarily increased without any discussion in the relevant file notings. When the Court asked him to show the exact page and provision of the policy supporting the claim, the ASG continued to rely on the alleged departure from the Dawan Committee's recommendations.

The Court directed the ASG to file fresh written submissions in a tabular format before the next hearing, setting out the specific challenges to the impugined order. The submissions are to identify.

1. The paragraphs of the impugned order under challenge, along with the corresponding grounds in the original revision petition.

2. The findings challenged.

3. Whether the challenge is that the wrong legal test was applied, or that material on record was ignored or misread, identifying such material by its page in the trial court record.

4. The respondents to whom each challenge relates.

Where no specific paragraph in the original revision petition covers a particular challenge, the same is also to be indicated. The submissions are to be filed at least two days before the next hearing, with an advance copy to counsel for all respondents.

The Court declined, for the present, to call for written submissions from the respondents. "I don't want multiple written submissions at this stage. Once you conclude, then it'll be better for them (respondents) to file it in one shot at that point of time," Justice Datta said.

The matter is listed for further consideration on November 5 at 2:30 PM.

What has happened so far in the Delhi Excise policy case

In July, the High Court had granted a last and final opportunity to [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4] and [ACCUSED_7] to file their replies in the CBI's revision petition.

Notably, on May 19, the Court had issued fresh notices to the three respondents. Earlier, Justice Sharma had rejected recusal pleas filed by [ACCUSED_6] and others, who had expressed apprehension of bias. She later decided to continue hearing the matter, prompting the accused to indicate that they would boycott proceedings before her.

The CBI’s revision petition challenges the trial court’s order dated February 27, which discharged all 23 accused in the case, including senior political leaders. The trial court had also made strong observations questioning aspects of the CBI’s investigation. In a detailed order, the court criticised the investigation conducted by the CBI, observing that the agency had implicated the accused without sufficient material.

The judge had noted that the voluminous chargesheet contained several lacunae and was not supported by witness statements or substantive evidence. The High Court had earlier observed that certain findings of the trial court appeared prima facie erroneous, leading to the CBI’s challenge in revision.

It is to be noted that Senior AAP leader [ACCUSED_4] had written to Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma of the Delhi High Court, stating that he will not participate in further hearings in the matter, citing concerns over the “appearance of impartial justice” and invoking principles of conscience and Satyagraha. [ACCUSED_4]’s letter follows a similar communication by [ACCUSED_6] a day earlier. Referring to it, [ACCUSED_4] stated, “I have carefully considered the substance of that letter… I find myself in respectful agreement with the stand taken by him, which is based on [OTHER_18]'s teachings on Satyagraha.”

[ACCUSED_4]'s recusal case involves a pending criminal revision petition before the Delhi High Court, where he had sought the recusal of Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma citing apprehensions of bias. In the same case, [ACCUSED_6] was permitted to argue the recusal plea in person and he had made detailed submissions before the Court.

The High Court, however, rejected the recusal plea, holding that the grounds raised did not justify withdrawal of the judge and cautioning against allegations that could undermine the institution’s integrity if not substantiated.

Following the hearing, videos of [ACCUSED_6]’s courtroom arguments surfaced and were widely circulated on social media, triggering a separate controversy over alleged unauthorised recording and dissemination of court proceedings. The same is under consideration before the High Court. It is in this backdrop that after [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4] and [ACCUSED_7] have written to the Court expressing their decision to abstain from further participation in the matter.

The Delhi High Court on Friday rejected a plea seeking a preliminary hearing on the objection to the maintainability of the Central Bureau of Investigation's (CBI) revision petition challenging the discharge of 23 accused persons in the alleged liquor policy scam case.

Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma dismissed the plea plea moved by one of the accused, [ACCUSED_2], seeking modification of the Court's earlier directions to ensure that his objection to the maintainability of the CBI's petition is heard and decided before the main matter is taken up on merits.

The Court said that while it does not doubt the sense of responsibility with which the learned senior counsel has approached the matter, the fact remains that the order in question was dictated in open Court and thereafter signed by Justice Sharma.

“The judicial record, which records the proceedings and submissions made before the Court, cannot be displaced merely on the basis of a subsequent assertion to the contrary. No objection was raised by the learned counsel at the time the order was dictated in their presence,” the Court said.

”The order was thereafter uploaded, and five months have elapsed since it was uploaded on the official website of the Delhi High Court, during which period no such application was moved, nor was any prayer made before the concerned Roster Bench seeking correction of the order or requesting that the matter be placed before this Court,” it added.

However, it clarified that rhe Roster Bench shall be at liberty to consider any other plea raised before it and that today's order shall not be construed as an expression of opinion on the merits of the preliminary objections to the maintainability of the revision petition.

The application challenges the direction passed on May 08 and reiterated on August 17 that preliminary objections to the maintainability of the revision petition would be considered along with the main petition.

[ACCUSED_2] has contended that the question of whether the revision petition was validly instituted must be decided at the threshold, before the Court examines the merits of the CBI's challenge to the discharge order.

[ACCUSED_2] has argued that deciding the maintainability objection first would conserve judicial time, particularly since the CBI's revision petition concerns 23 respondents.

On February 27, the trial court discharged all the 23 accused persons in the case, including political leaders [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4] and [ACCUSED_26]. The trial court had also severely criticised the CBI's investigation in the case.

It may be noted that the case had become politically controversial, as [ACCUSED_6] was arrested and remanded to the custody amidst the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. He was latergranted bail by the Supreme Court after 156 days of custody. AAP leader [ACCUSED_4] also spent 530 days in custody in the case.

The CBI's revision against the trial court's order was heard by Justice Sharma, who on March 9, prima facie observed that the trial court's observations were erroneous.

Later, [ACCUSED_6] and some other accused, including [ACCUSED_4], filed applications seeking recusal of Justice Sharma on ground of apprehension of bias. Justice Sharma, dismissed the recusal applications and decided to hear the matter herself.

Thereafter, [ACCUSED_6] and [ACCUSED_4] wrote to Justice Sharma stating that they are boycotting the hearing before her and will not appear, either in person or through a counsel.

The matter was transferred to Justice Jain later. However, today's application was listed before Justice Sharma as it sought clarification of order passed by her.

Justice Sharma initiated contempt proceedingsagainst [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4], [ACCUSED_9], [ACCUSED_27], [ACCUSED_7] and [ACCUSED_28]. She had earlier rejected the recusal applications filed by [ACCUSED_6] and others.

documents.title: 'Judicial Discipline': Judge Says Another Bench To Hear [ACCUSED_6] Case
documents.text:
New Delhi: 
Days after refusing to recuse herself from hearing a CBI petition against [ACCUSED_6] and others in the liquor policy case, Delhi High Court judge Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma on Thursday said the plea would now be heard by another bench. The judge, who initiated contempt proceedings against [ACCUSED_6] and other top AAP leaders after making scorching remarks against them, made it clear that her action shouldn't be construed as allowing the party chief's plea for recusal.

Justice Sharma said the excise policy case will be heard by another bench, clarifying that since she has initiated contempt proceedings, it is appropriate that the matter be transferred to some other judge.

"For a judge who is being targeted is a very lonely battle...This is not recusal. This is judicial discipline," Justice Sharma observed.

[ACCUSED_6], one of the prime accused in the liquor policy case, had sought the judge's recusal because she had allegedly taken part in events linked to the RSS. He further cited past orders of the high court in the same case, rejecting bail pleas which he said were later turned over by the Supreme Court. AAP leaders also flagged that the children of the judge were empanelled with Solicitor General Tushar Mehta.

However, Justice Sharma refused to recuse herself, asserting that there was no material to substantiate claims of bias.

The former Delhi chief minister hadn't been appearing in the liquor policy case before the Delhi High Court, alleging bias on Justice Sharma's part.

The judge today ordered contempt proceedings against [ACCUSED_6], [ACCUSED_4], [ACCUSED_7], [ACCUSED_9], [ACCUSED_27], [ACCUSED_31] and [ACCUSED_32], saying "extremely vilifying, extremely contemptuous, and defamatory material" was being spread online by these leaders, amounting to an attack on the judiciary.

Justice Sharma said that "a parallel narrative was being constructed outside through a digital campaign" by contemnors "armed with political powers".

"My family members were dragged and vilified with edited videos... It was to intimidate not only me but the institution of the judiciary," added the judge.

[ACCUSED_6] had recently shared a video on X, saying he didn't hope to get justice from the judge.

"My hope of receiving justice from Justice Swarnkanta Sharma Ji has been shattered... Listening to the voice of my conscience, adhering to the principles of Gandhi Ji, and with the spirit of Satyagraha, I have decided that I will not appear before her in this case and will not present any arguments either," his post read.

Institution Put On Trial: Justice Sharma

The judge said on Thursday that she was trained to accept criticism, but it was her duty as a judge to ensure that the court was not governed by such allegations.

"When the institution is put on trial, it becomes the duty of the judge to ensure that the court is not governed by such allegations," the judge said.

"I am trained to accept fair criticism and dissent... The robe worn by the judge demands calmness... However, sometimes remaining silent is not judicial restraint. The moment has arrived today," she added.

She also said that [ACCUSED_6] was trying to intimidate her.

Earlier this month, Justice Sharma refused to accede to [ACCUSED_6]'s plea for her recusal.

"If I recused myself today, I would be abandoning my duty. [ACCUSED_6] has said so many times while arguing that he is not doubting my integrity, but he has doubts in his mind. Such illusions in the mind of [ACCUSED_6] cannot be ground for recusal," Justice Sharma had said.

judgment.facts: This judgment decides recusal requests by six discharged accused in the CBI's revision challenging the Delhi Excise Policy discharge order, not the merits of the alleged offences. The court found that advance copies had been served on their Trial Court counsel, who also represented them in the High Court, and that the discharge order had never been stayed. It found that earlier arrest and bail observations were provisional and that neither attendance at legal events nor relatives' government-panel work established a connection with the dispute or an interest in its outcome.
judgment.motive: No motive for the underlying alleged offences was determined in this recusal judgment. The court characterized the recusal requests as resting on conjecture and subjective apprehensions, and considered that accepting such grounds would enable forum shopping.
judgment.trigger: The principal immediate procedural trigger was the interim order of 09.03.2026, whose preliminary observations and limited relief the applicants said created an apprehension of bias. Other asserted grounds concerned earlier judgments, professional events, relatives' government-panel engagements, and public or social-media statements.
judgment.court_reasoning: The court applied an objective reasonable-apprehension standard and held that subjective unease, unsupported suspicion, and adverse interim orders did not establish grounds for recusal. Earlier arrest and bail decisions involved different legal tests and expressly provisional observations, rather than a final determination of guilt. The court found no tangible nexus between the judge's relatives' professional engagements and this case, and no political statement or conduct supporting the allegation based on attendance at legal events. It held that unjustified withdrawal would undermine judicial independence and permit litigants to influence bench selection.
judgment.outcome: All recusal applications, including the oral request considered for Respondent No. 5, were rejected. The judge retained the case and stated that the main revision would be heard independently on its merits, unaffected by the recusal applications. No conviction, acquittal, or sentence was pronounced; the accused remained discharged pending determination of the revision.
